title: Clinical Trials in Practice
subtitle: From Foundations to AI Agents
full_title: Clinical Trials in Practice: From Foundations to AI Agents
short_description: Clinical trials as science and as regulated operations: design and statistics, the daily work of a Phase III study from site selection to the trial master file, regulatory submission, and what AI agents may and may not do in regulated research.
description:
On an open highway you can pass every other car and go as fast as the engine allows. A clinical trial is downtown driving. The pace is set by the traffic around you: regulators, sites, patients, and the protocol itself. Speed that ignores that traffic does not get you there sooner.

This book explains how that traffic moves and how to work with it. It follows a trial from the first idea to the regulatory submission and gives Phase III the most room, because that is where approval is won or lost. Statistics, operations and technology are taught side by side, because a design choice in the protocol becomes a task at the site, a field in the database and a document an inspector will ask to see.

Some of the questions it answers: When does a study need an IND, and what does an investigator take on by becoming the sponsor of one? How do you size a trial, plan interim analyses, and decide whether an adaptive or Bayesian design is worth the extra planning? When can real world evidence or an external control arm support a regulatory decision? Why does a site that predicts 30 patients sometimes enroll 3, and how should a sponsor read feasibility data? What does an academic multi-site trial need from its coordinating center, and what does a site new to research, rural or urban, usually lack? What does risk-based monitoring change about a monitor's work? What has to be in the trial master file when the inspector arrives?

The chapters run in the order a development program does. They begin with how clinical research took its present shape, from the Elixir Sulfanilamide deaths of 1937 to ICH E6(R3) Good Clinical Practice, and with the ethics of research with human subjects. They follow a compound through development economics and Phases I to IV. The Phase III part covers statistical methods, adaptive and Bayesian trial design with platform trials such as I-SPY 2 and REMAP-CAP, study design and protocol complexity, randomization and blinding, endpoints and estimands, site selection, patient recruitment and retention, logistics and project management, data management and EDC, clinical monitoring, safety reporting, essential documents and the trial master file, and the IT systems underneath. The last chapters cover closeout, the clinical study report, and regulatory submission, including expedited pathways and FDA inspections.

The chapter on AI agents treats an agent as one more computerized system that must survive an inspection. It sets out what FDA and EMA guidance allows today, such as TMF filing, query generation and eligibility prescreening as decision support, and what it does not allow, such as replacing the investigator's judgment. It describes how structured, machine-readable protocols (ICH M11, CDISC USDM) connect the protocol to data collection, and it says plainly where no measured evidence exists yet. Every use it describes needs validation, an audit trail and a named person accountable for each decision.

It is written for medical directors, study managers and monitors; for investigators and site coordinators, including those running their own investigator-initiated trials; for statisticians who want to see how a design plays out in practice; and for students and informatics and AI engineers who need to know how regulated research works before they build tools for it.

chapters.title: Historical Context and Evolution
chapters.summary:
Why do clinical trials follow the rules they do? The chapter links the main protections of modern trials to the events that preceded them: the Elixir Sulfanilamide deaths and the 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the Nuremberg Code, thalidomide and the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Drug Amendments, the Declaration of Helsinki, the Tuskegee Syphilis Study, and the Belmont Report with the Common Rule. It then follows the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) and its Good Clinical Practice (GCP) guideline E6 through the R2 and R3 revisions, and records recent developments, mainly Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance on decentralized trials, adaptive and Bayesian designs, real world evidence, master protocols and Diversity Action Plans, plus the start of the EU Clinical Trials Information System (CTIS). A reader can match each protection (safety testing of drugs, voluntary consent, independent review by an institutional review board, proof of efficacy) to its event and see which current guidance is final and which is a draft.

chapters.title: Lifecycle of a Clinical Trial
chapters.summary:
What stages does a clinical trial pass through, and where does it sit in drug development? The chapter maps the sequence from discovery and preclinical testing through the Investigational New Drug (IND) application or Clinical Trial Application (CTA), Phase I to Phase IV, submission, review and approval. It tabulates the question, typical size, duration and key decisions of each phase, and reports likelihood of approval from Phase I in a Biotechnology Innovation Organization analysis of 2011 to 2020 programs (oncology 5.3%, programs outside oncology 9.3%). It presents the 4DM (Drug Discovery, Development and Deployment Map) as an alternative to the linear pipeline. It then follows one Phase III trial through planning and design, startup, execution and closeout, up to the Clinical Study Report (CSR) and a Marketing Authorization Application (MAA), New Drug Application (NDA) or Biologics License Application (BLA), and names four cross cutting concerns: regulatory compliance, ethics, quality and data integrity (the ALCOA principles: attributable, legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate), and economic constraints. A reader can place the main operational tasks of a trial in their stage and find the book chapter that treats each.

chapters.title: Regulatory Framework
chapters.summary:
Which rules govern a clinical trial in the United States and internationally? The chapter covers the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER), Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research (CBER) and Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH); the Code of Federal Regulations parts for trials (21 CFR Parts 11, 50, 56 and 312); the Investigational New Drug (IND) application, with its 30 day review and clinical hold; and the duties of sponsor, contract research organization (CRO), investigator and institutional review board (IRB). It then covers International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidelines (E6 Good Clinical Practice, E8, E9, M4), the EU Clinical Trials Regulation, essential documents and the Trial Master File, FDA inspection outcomes from no action indicated to official action indicated, and the governance of AI and automation in regulated trials. A further section gives regulatory expectations for adaptive and Bayesian designs, including the 2019 FDA guidance, ICH E20 and simulation as evidence. A reader can decide which center and IND route apply, how long to keep records, and what to agree with FDA before enrolling.

chapters.title: Ethical Principles
chapters.summary:
What makes clinical research ethical, beyond informed consent? The chapter presents the seven requirements of Emanuel, Wendler and Grady (value, scientific validity, fair subject selection, favorable risk benefit ratio, independent review, informed consent, respect for participants), then shows where they collide in practice: placebo controls under the Declaration of Helsinki, clinical equipoise, vulnerable populations under the Common Rule (45 CFR 46), and research in resource limited settings. It takes up data privacy in decentralized trials, electronic informed consent (eConsent) under Food and Drug Administration (FDA) guidance, and AI and automation, covering bias auditing, transparency in consent and accountability. A closing section describes institutional review board (IRB) review: initial, continuing (at least annually), modification, adverse event and final review, and the decisive authority of the IRB. A reader can test a design, a population choice or an AI use against the seven requirements and plan the safeguards and IRB reviews.

chapters.title: Overview of Drug Development
chapters.summary:
This chapter answers how a compound moves from discovery to an approved medicine, and why most compounds that reach human testing do not complete the path. It follows preclinical research, the Investigational New Drug (IND) filing with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), the four clinical phases, and regulatory review. It sets Phase I to IV beside the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E8(R1) classification of studies by objective and its Critical to Quality (CtQ) factors. It covers expedited programs (Fast Track, Breakthrough Therapy, Accelerated Approval, Priority Review), the Target Product Profile (TPP), and attrition: about 28% of programs pass from Phase II to Phase III, and about 7% of programs starting Phase I reach the market (2020 to 2024 averages). A reader can place a study in the phase and objective framework, see which expedited programs can be combined, and read stage success rates when judging risk.

chapters.title: Economics of a Trial
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks what clinical trials cost, who pays, and how those economics shape drug development. It reports estimates of what it costs to develop a drug through approval (the 2025 Deloitte cohort average is $2.67 billion), critiques of the Tufts estimate, costs by phase, and the cost of a day of delay. It follows money from sponsors to contract research organizations (CROs), sites and vendors, and covers site budgets, patient out of pocket costs, trial globalization and the rise of China. It also explains how artificial intelligence and automation can change cost structure, funding interim analyses, predictive probability of success (PPoS), assurance as against power, and platform trial economics. A reader can compare cost benchmarks with their assumptions, build a site budget, specify a funding checkpoint, and judge a program on assurance rather than power.

chapters.title: Phase I: Human Pharmacology
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains how a first human dose is chosen and what Phase I studies measure. It covers starting dose selection from the NOAEL (no observed adverse effect level), reduced by a default safety factor of 10, and from the MABEL (minimal anticipated biological effect level), with the 2006 TGN1412 case as the warning. It covers sentinel dosing and stopping rules for first in human trials, single and multiple ascending dose studies, pharmacokinetic parameters, and special studies such as bioequivalence and thorough QT. For oncology it compares the 3+3 design with BOIN (Bayesian optimal interval), CRM (continual reassessment method) and BLRM (Bayesian logistic regression model), adds EWOC (escalation with overdose control), and explains Project Optimus and combination escalation. A reader can choose a starting dose framework, write dose limiting toxicity definitions and stopping rules, and simulate an escalation design before the trial begins.

chapters.title: Phase II: Exploratory
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains what Phase II must establish: whether a drug produces a worthwhile therapeutic effect, and at what dose it goes into Phase III. About 70% of drugs entering Phase II do not advance to Phase III. It separates Phase IIa proof of concept from Phase IIb dose finding, and covers dose response, the Emax model, MCP-Mod and Bayesian adaptive dose finding, surrogate endpoints, the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E9(R1) estimands framework, clinical outcome assessments and biomarkers. It also covers adaptive designs, futility stopping by conditional power and predictive probability of success (PPoS), and the go or no go decision. A reader can choose a dose finding approach, state an estimand for a surrogate endpoint, prespecify a futility rule and check it by simulation, and weigh efficacy, safety, dose and commercial viability before Phase III.

chapters.title: Phase III: Confirmatory
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains what Phase III confirmatory trials must show and how they are designed, monitored and justified for approval. It compares Phase II and Phase III trials, and covers the choice of control (placebo or active, superiority or noninferiority), the estimand and its five attributes under the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E9(R1), and the statistical analysis plan. It explains interim analyses and group sequential designs (O'Brien-Fleming, Pocock and Lan-DeMets boundaries), futility stopping, the two pivotal trial paradigm and the single trial standard, and designs that join Phase II and III in one trial. It covers ICH E1 safety exposure for long term treatment (about 1500 patients), Data Safety Monitoring Boards (DSMBs), ICH E5 bridging studies, and Diversity Action Plans. A reader can choose a control and estimand, plan interim looks without inflating Type I error, and judge when one pivotal trial may suffice.

chapters.title: Phase IV: Post-Marketing Studies and Surveillance
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains what is studied and monitored after approval, and which of those studies a sponsor can be compelled to complete. It classifies Phase IV studies (post marketing safety and efficacy studies, requirements and commitments, label extensions, outcomes research) and describes how FDORA (Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act, 2022) lets the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) require a confirmatory trial to be underway before, or within a set period after, accelerated approval. It covers pharmacovigilance through spontaneous reporting (FAERS and AEMS, its replacement launched in March 2026) and active surveillance (Sentinel System; DARWIN EU, the Data Analysis and Real World Interrogation Network), Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies (REMS), comparative effectiveness research, patient registries, real world evidence, health technology assessment and lifecycle management. A reader can tell required from voluntary studies, see where a spontaneous report signal is confirmed, and identify the evidence payers ask for.

chapters.title: Statistical Methods for Clinical Trials
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains how a confirmatory trial separates a modest treatment effect from large uncontrolled variation, and which frequentist methods support the comparison. It covers hypothesis testing, Type I error, power and sample size; intent to treat and the estimands framework of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E9(R1); survival analysis (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank, Cox, restricted mean survival time, competing risks); analysis of covariance and mixed models for repeated measures (MMRM); missing data (missing at random versus not at random, multiple imputation, tipping point analysis); group sequential designs with alpha spending, futility rules and the promising zone design; sequential multiple assignment randomized trials (SMART) for dynamic treatment regimes; and causal inference from observational data (propensity scores, target trial emulation, marginal structural models, E-values). A reader can choose an estimand and a missing data strategy before enrollment, allocate alpha across interim looks, and judge whether a SMART is justified.

chapters.title: Adaptive and Bayesian Trial Design
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how trials can learn from accumulating data while keeping Type I error under control, and why fixed designs strain under precision medicine, rare diseases and many treatment options. It builds from the bandit problem (Thompson sampling, dynamic programming) and Bayesian updating with Beta priors, through early Bayesian adaptive trials (CALGB 49907, ASTIN), Phase II/III dose selection (AWARD-5), an adaptive Phase II trial (lecanemab) and a platform trial (I-SPY 2), to hierarchical models that borrow information across tumor types in basket trials. It also covers predictive probabilities, administrative analyses, simulation of operating characteristics, Type I error in Bayesian trials, response adaptive randomization, and guidance from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), including the 2026 Bayesian draft, draft E20 and the one trial standard. A reader can judge where response adaptive randomization pays and what simulation a regulator expects.

chapters.title: Study Design
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks which design choices, made before the first patient is enrolled, let an observed effect be credited to the intervention. It covers randomization (simple, block, stratified), levels of blinding, placebo, active, historical and external controls, digital twins, Bayesian borrowing, parallel, crossover, factorial, cluster and stepped wedge designs, and the four inputs to sample size. It then treats master protocols (basket, umbrella and platform trials), the arithmetic of a shared control arm, and case studies: REMAP-CAP, COVID-19 anticoagulation platforms, SNAP, PANTHER, Healey ALS and EPAD. It closes with the statistical analysis plan, the estimands addendum of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH), the protocol (ICH E6(R3), SPIRIT 2025, ICH M11) and protocol amendments under Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Union rules, with Tufts CSDD benchmarks. A reader can compare design types, estimate the enrollment a shared control arm saves, and plan protocol amendments.

chapters.title: Real-World Evidence and Evidence Integration
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks when real world data can support regulatory and payer decisions as real world evidence (RWE), and how to design and analyze such studies. It covers the United States framework (the 21st Century Cures Act, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) 2018 framework, fit for purpose), the European Medicines Agency's DARWIN EU, health technology assessment and managed entry agreements, and data sources (electronic health records, claims, registries, Sentinel). Designs include external and synthetic control arms, hybrid randomized designs with power, meta analytic predictive (MAP) or commensurate priors, registry based randomized trials and embedded pragmatic trials. Methods include the active comparator new user design, immortal time bias, propensity scores, instrumental variables, difference in differences, regression discontinuity, E-values and negative controls. Cases include palbociclib in male breast cancer, where FDA treated the real world data as supportive rather than primary, and COVID-19 vaccine effectiveness. A reader can decide when RWE belongs in a development program.

chapters.title: Protocol Design Benchmarks
chapters.summary:
How large and complex are clinical trial protocols, how has that changed, and what does complexity cost? The chapter reports Tufts Center for the Study of Drug Development (Tufts CSDD) benchmarks by phase, for oncology against other protocols, and for rare disease against other protocols: endpoints, eligibility criteria, procedures, visits, countries, sites, datapoints, completion rate, and time from protocol finalization to database lock. It separates core procedures (those that serve a primary or key secondary endpoint) from noncore ones, reports that heavier protocols tend to show lower recruitment, retention and adherence and more deviations and amendments, and lists drivers of complexity. It separates protocol completion from loss of outcome follow up, which sample size planning allows for, and links the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E6(R3) guideline to proportionate trial processes. The data predate the pandemic and are best read as a floor. A reader can compare a draft protocol with these benchmarks and decide which noncore procedures to challenge.

chapters.title: Randomization and Blinding
chapters.summary:
How do randomization and blinding protect a trial from bias, and which methods suit which trials? The chapter compares simple, block, stratified block, minimization (dynamic allocation), response adaptive randomization (RAR), covariate adaptive and cluster randomization by information needed, balance and predictability. It explains allocation concealment, interactive response technology (IRT), treatment crossover, and the blinding provisions of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E6(R3) guideline. It covers open label, single blind, double blind and triple blind designs, side effects that reveal assignment, and sham procedures and active comparators for device and behavioral trials. The randomized play the winner rule, Thompson sampling and the neonatal extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) trials illustrate RAR, for which equal randomization is generally preferred in confirmatory Phase III trials with two arms. A reader can choose an allocation method, plan concealment and blinding, and judge when adaptive allocation is defensible.

chapters.title: Endpoints and Outcomes
chapters.summary:
Which outcome should a trial measure to demonstrate that a drug works, and how does that choice shape design, sample size and regulatory strategy? The chapter sets out the hierarchy of clinical endpoints, surrogate endpoints and biomarkers, including overall survival, progression free survival, patient reported outcomes (PROs) and their validation, and digital health technology (DHT) endpoints. It shows how surrogates can mislead (the Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial, CAST, and hormone therapy), how reasonably likely surrogates can support accelerated approval by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for serious conditions, and how minimal residual disease (MRD) and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) are being studied. It covers primary and secondary endpoints, multiplicity, composite and time to event endpoints, ordinal endpoints, the win ratio, desirability of outcome ranking (DOOR), and the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E9(R1) estimands framework with its strategies for intercurrent events such as death. A reader can choose an endpoint and state its estimand.

chapters.title: Site Selection and Feasibility
chapters.summary:
How does a sponsor find, assess and activate the clinical research sites that will actually enroll patients? The chapter covers site identification (access to patients, geographic distribution, prior experience), the falling number of U.S. investigators and the one and done pattern, and Diversity Action Plans under the Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act (FDORA) of 2022, whose guidance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has been in flux. It presents the feasibility assessment with its criteria and red flags, the tendency of sites to overestimate enrollment, and the Clinical Trial Agreement (CTA), site budget and coverage analysis that stand between a qualified and an activated site. It reports 2024 WCG survey data on startup bottlenecks by site type, then the site initiation visit (SIV) and global trials. A reader can screen candidate sites against explicit criteria, discount investigator enrollment estimates, and plan contracts and budgets.

chapters.title: Patient Recruitment and Retention
chapters.summary:
Why do trials struggle to recruit and retain participants, and what can sponsors and sites do about it? The chapter treats recruitment as an attrition problem, with an illustrative funnel, and compares provider referral, community outreach, direct advertising, social media, registries and decentralized elements. It covers barriers, geographic access for rural patients, retention, investigator and coordinator attrition, representative enrollment, and metrics such as screen failure rate and enrollment rate. A large section treats AI and machine learning enabled recruitment: identification from electronic health records (EHRs) with computable phenotypes, Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) and its OMOP Common Data Model, SMART on FHIR, conversational agents, electronic informed consent, and the SPIRIT-AI, CONSORT-AI and TRIPOD+AI reporting extensions. A reader can plan recruitment channels, set tracking metrics, and judge the risks of AI tools that decide who is contacted.

chapters.title: Logistics and Project Management
chapters.summary:
How are the people, documents, supplies and processes of a clinical trial coordinated so that a protocol becomes executed research? The chapter covers the roles of sponsor, principal investigator, contract research organization (CRO) and study coordinator, delegation and accountability under 21 CFR Part 312 and U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Form 1572, partner selection by request for proposal, and biospecimen chain of custody. It relates the protocol to standard operating procedures (SOPs), and describes the Trial Master File (TMF) and Investigator Site File. It gives development timelines and success rates, multiregional clinical trials under International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidelines E5 and E17, startup bottlenecks, and project management by scope, schedule, budget, quality and critical path. It also treats direct to patient and decentralized trials, Good Publication Practice (GPP 2022), and an ancillary study policy aligned with the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Policy for Data Management and Sharing. A reader can set delegation and oversight, plan timelines and budgets, and choose an execution model.

chapters.title: Data Management
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains how observations made at a trial site become data that a regulator can trust and trace back to source. It follows the clinical data management pipeline: electronic data capture (EDC), edit checks, audit trails, queries, source documents, eSource, source data verification (SDV) and database lock. It covers data arriving outside EDC (central laboratories, imaging, wearables, real world data) and a data transfer specification checklist. It presents common data elements, the ALCOA, ALCOA+ and ALCOA++ integrity principles, Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) standards, and the traceability chain to the electronic Common Technical Document (eCTD). Compliance topics are 21 CFR Part 11, computer system validation, and records retention under U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and European Union rules. A reader can plan data capture and cleaning, specify external transfers, and test whether a submitted number traces to source.

chapters.title: Clinical Monitoring
chapters.summary:
This chapter asks how a sponsor keeps a running trial safe, competent and compliant with Good Clinical Practice (GCP), and how that oversight is checked from outside. It describes the clinical research associate (CRA), the four visit types (qualification, initiation, interim monitoring, closeout), source data verification (SDV), source document review and the monitoring report. It presents risk based quality management (RBQM): risk assessment, quality tolerance limits, key risk indicators, and centralized, remote and hybrid monitoring. It separates quality control, quality assurance, sponsor audits and regulatory inspections, with an inspection readiness checklist, Form 483 from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and corrective and preventive action (CAPA). It closes with governance committees: data safety monitoring boards (DSMB), including platform trials, endpoint adjudication committees and steering committees. A reader can draft a risk based monitoring plan and prepare for inspection.

chapters.title: Safety Monitoring and Reporting
chapters.summary:
This chapter answers how adverse events in a clinical trial are classified, reported and interpreted, and which reporting clocks apply. It defines adverse event (AE), serious adverse event (SAE), adverse drug reaction (ADR), suspected unexpected serious adverse reaction (SUSAR) and adverse event of special interest (AESI), and separates seriousness from severity, most often graded on the CTCAE scale (Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events). It sets out investigator and sponsor duties: immediate SAE reporting, expedited reports to regulators within 7 or 15 calendar days, safety reports to investigators, and the annual Development Safety Update Report (DSUR). It covers reconciliation of safety and clinical databases, laboratory safety analysis, signal detection, reporting rules of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Union, which rest on International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E2A and E2B, and benefit risk assessment. A reader can classify an event, find its reporting deadline and choose analyses for finding a safety signal.

chapters.title: Essential Documents and the Trial Master File
chapters.summary:
This chapter answers what documentation shows that a trial was conducted properly, where each document is kept, and how long it is retained. It defines essential documents under International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E6(R2) and the essential records of ICH E6(R3), and separates the sponsor's trial master file (TMF) from the investigator site file (ISF) and the electronic site file (eISF). chapters.title: Clinical Trial IT Infrastructure
chapters.summary:
This chapter answers which computerized systems a clinical trial runs on and what makes them defensible in an inspection. It describes the four core platforms, EDC (electronic data capture), CTMS (clinical trial management system), eTMF (electronic trial master file) and RTSM (randomization and trial supply management, also called interactive response technology), and how they connect in single vendor and mixed vendor stacks. chapters.title: AI Agents in Clinical Development

This chapter asks where artificial intelligence (AI) agents can be used in clinical development and what regulators require first. chapters.title: Trial Closeout and Analysis
chapters.summary:
This chapter covers the period after the last patient last visit (LPLV) and up to the end of a trial, and how to interpret the result. It sets out the closeout sequence: query resolution, medical coding, database lock, a statistical analysis plan (SAP) finalized before unblinding, and the analysis that feeds the clinical study report (CSR). It argues that a result is evidence to weigh rather than a binary verdict, using the COVID anticoagulation multiplatform trial and the aducanumab Phase III program as cases, and says to report effect sizes and confidence intervals against the minimum clinically important difference. It then covers site closeout and investigational product (IP) accounting, a checklist for closing out computerized systems and external data flows, results posting to ClinicalTrials.gov under the Food and Drug Administration Amendments Act (FDAAA 801), data sharing, and post hoc analyses. It classifies trial failures as efficacy, safety or operational, lists the costs of delay, and describes artificial intelligence (AI) as a way to reduce reconciliation work under governance. chapters.title: The Clinical Study Report
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains what a clinical study report (CSR) is, who reads it, how it is written and how its results should be reported. It presents the structure of the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E3 guideline with typical page lengths, and the writing process: medical writers working from the statistical analysis plan, the locked database and tables, listings and figures (TLFs), early drafting of a shell, and when an abbreviated CSR is acceptable. It covers disclosure: the summary of results for laypersons under EU Clinical Trials Regulation 536/2014, European Medicines Agency (EMA) Policy 0070 with its anonymization report, and the oseltamivir (Tamiflu) reanalysis based on full CSRs. It then covers reporting against the prespecified estimand under ICH E9(R1), Bayesian results as posterior probabilities with credible intervals (the REBYOTA review is the example), communicating uncertainty, and adaptive and platform trial reports, and places the CSR in Module 5 of the Common Technical Document. chapters.title: Regulatory Submission
chapters.summary:
This chapter explains how a sponsor builds, submits and defends a marketing application, mainly in the United States, and how other regions differ. It defines the New Drug Application (NDA), Biologics License Application (BLA), Abbreviated New Drug Application (ANDA), Marketing Authorization Application (MAA) and the Common Technical Document (CTD) with its five modules. It covers FDA meeting types, expedited programs, the 2022 Food and Drug Omnibus Reform Act (FDORA) changes to accelerated approval, and the review cycle: refuse to file decisions, Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) goals, advisory committees, Bioresearch Monitoring (BIMO) inspections and complete response letters. A long section examines approval on a single trial: the 0.025 squared false positive probability behind the two trial rule, Fisher's method, the 1997 Food and Drug Administration Modernization Act (FDAMA) exception, five supporting features, the loss of breadth and the June 2026 revised draft guidance. It closes with the European, Japanese and Chinese pathways and postmarketing obligations. A reader can choose a pathway and judge whether one pivotal trial could support approval.

- FDAMA single trial provision, 21 U.S.C. 355(d) (United States Congress 1997)
- One pivotal trial as the new FDA default (Prasad and Makary 2026)

chapters.title: Glossary and Abbreviations
chapters.summary:
This appendix is the book's reference list of abbreviations and of statistical and clinical trial terms. The abbreviations table gives each term in full with a short definition, listed alphabetically and covering regulators and agencies (FDA, EMA, PMDA, NMPA), regulatory submissions (NDA, BLA, MAA, CTD, eCTD), good practice and quality (GCP, GMP, GLP, GAMP, ALCOA), data standards and systems (CDISC, SDTM, ADaM, EDC, CTMS, IRT), safety reporting and monitoring (SAE, ADR, SUSAR, DSMB) and artificial intelligence (LLM, RAG, MCP). The statistical terms table defines alpha, power, Type I and Type II error, p-value, confidence interval, estimand, intercurrent events, hazard ratio, Bayesian and frequentist approaches, and master protocol designs. Most entries carry no citation. A few name their source: International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) E2A for adverse drug reaction and serious adverse event, ICH E6 for Good Clinical Practice (GCP) and the trial master file, and 21 CFR 312.40 for the Investigational New Drug (IND) application. A reader can look up an abbreviation or term as the book defines it.
